subject: chemistry
title: Heat energy change and molar enthalpy
key_idea: The heat energy change is found from Q = mcΔT. The molar enthalpy change, ΔH, is the heat energy change per mole, in kJ/mol. ΔH is negative when the temperature rises (exothermic) and positive when it falls (endothermic).

blocks.text: When a reaction happens in water, the temperature change of the water tells you the heat energy change.

blocks.label: Heat energy change
where: Q = heat energy change in J
m = mass of water or solution in g (1.0 cm³ of water has a mass of 1.0 g)
c = specific heat capacity in J/g/°C (4.2 for water, or the value given in the question)

items.text: Use the mass of water or solution that was heated, not the mass of the solid or fuel.
50 cm³ of water rises by 8.0 °C: Q = 50 × 4.2 × 8.0 = 1680 J.

diagram.alt: Practise calculating the heat energy change Q from the mass of water and the temperature change.
diagram.question: **{m} g** of water is heated and its temperature rises by **{t} °C**. The specific heat capacity of water is 4.2 J/g/°C. Calculate the heat energy change, Q, in J.

items: Q = mcΔT, with m the mass of water in g.
Q is in joules when c is in J/g/°C.

blocks.text: The molar enthalpy change is the heat energy change for one mole of the reacting substance.

items.meaning: The heat energy change per mole of a substance, in kJ/mol.

blocks.label: Molar enthalpy change
where: ΔH = molar enthalpy change in kJ/mol
Q = heat energy change in kJ (J ÷ 1000)
n = amount of substance in mol (mass ÷ Mr)

items: If the temperature rises, the reaction is exothermic and ΔH is **negative**.
If the temperature falls, the reaction is endothermic and ΔH is **positive**.

items.text: Divide the mass of the reacting substance by its Mr or Ar.
Negative if the temperature rose, positive if it fell.

items: Example: 0.60 g of magnesium (Ar = 24) reacts with excess acid and Q = 11 500 J. The temperature rises.
The temperature rose, so ΔH = −460 kJ/mol.

diagram.alt: Practise calculating a molar enthalpy change from a temperature rise and the amount in moles.
diagram.question: **100 cm³** of solution (c = 4.2 J/g/°C, 1.0 cm³ has a mass of 1.0 g) rises in temperature by **{t} °C** when **{n} mol** of a reactant reacts. Calculate ΔH in kJ/mol, including the sign.
working: Q = 100 × 4.2 × {t} J, then ÷ 1000 to give kJ
The temperature rises, so the sign is negative: ΔH = **{answer}** kJ/mol

items: ΔH = Q ÷ n, with Q in kJ.
Exothermic gives a negative ΔH. Endothermic gives a positive ΔH.
Check the units: J ÷ 1000 gives kJ.

sections.heading: Burning a fuel to heat water

blocks.text: A fuel in a spirit burner can heat water in a copper can. The experiment gives the molar enthalpy change of combustion.

items.text: Find the mass of the spirit burner and fuel.
Burn the fuel under a known mass of water, stirring.
Immediately find the final mass of the burner and fuel.
Mass of fuel burned gives n. The water's temperature rise gives Q.

items: Stir the water so that the heat is spread evenly.
Weigh the burner straight away, so that no fuel evaporates.
The result is lower than the data book value, because heat is lost to the surroundings, combustion is incomplete, or the fuel is impure or evaporates.
The fuel burned gives n and the water's temperature rise gives Q.
Heat loss makes the measured value smaller than the data book value.

checks.q: Calculate Q when 100 g of water rises in temperature by 10 °C (c = 4.2 J/g/°C).
A reaction releases 4200 J when 0.020 mol reacts. Calculate ΔH in kJ/mol.
State the sign of ΔH when the temperature of the mixture falls.
checks.a: Positive, because the reaction is endothermic.

worked_example.question: The reaction between zinc and silver nitrate solution is exothermic. A mass of 0.65 g of zinc is added to excess silver nitrate solution. The heat energy change is 800 J. Calculate the molar enthalpy change, ΔH, in kJ/mol. Include a sign in your answer.
worked_example.tip: The question says exothermic, so the sign is negative. The answer without a minus sign loses a mark.
